items.title: RESPECT women: Preventing violence against women
items.author: WHO and UN partners · English
sections: Purpose and scope

A prevention framework explaining how governments, communities and organisations can reduce violence before it occurs by combining evidence-based strategies rather than relying on awareness campaigns alone.
Key guidance
Strengthen relationship skills through age-appropriate education on consent, communication, conflict and equality.
Empower women socially and economically while monitoring for backlash and pairing economic programmes with gender-transformative work.
Ensure survivor services are available and trusted; prevention messages can increase disclosure and demand for help.
Reduce poverty and economic stress through social protection, safe employment and access to resources.
Make schools, workplaces, transport and public spaces safer through policy, design, reporting and accountability.
Prevent child and adolescent abuse and interrupt the intergenerational transmission of violence.
Transform harmful gender norms through sustained community work that includes influential leaders without giving them control over women’s voices.
Use multiple coordinated strategies, local data and outcome evaluation; one-off campaigns rarely change violence rates.
How to use this guide

This guide turns the source publication into a practical reading aid. It is designed for survivors, trusted supporters, health and social-service staff, and programme managers. It does not replace emergency services, medical care, legal advice, or the complete source publication.

Use only the parts that fit the person’s situation. Preserve her choice, privacy and pace. If a suggested action could expose browsing, calls, documents or location to an abusive person, first choose a safer device, place or time.
Survivor-centred principles
Safety comes first. Ask what would make the next hours or days safer and avoid steps that may provoke retaliation. Never require a disclosure in order to offer basic help.
Respect autonomy and informed consent. Explain realistic options, benefits, limits and possible risks; the survivor decides what happens next unless an immediate legal safeguarding duty applies.
Protect confidentiality. Collect the minimum information, restrict access, agree on safe contact methods and explain any limits before information is shared.
Provide equitable access. Consider disability, language, age, migration status, poverty, rural isolation, sexual orientation and other barriers without stereotyping.
Practical response sequence
Begin with immediate safety and urgent health needs. Ask privately, without the suspected perpetrator present, whether it is safe to talk and whether the person needs emergency care.
Listen without interrogation. Validate what happened, avoid blame, and do not demand a chronological account or proof. Record only what is necessary and use the survivor’s own words.

Offer a small number of verified options: medical care, safe accommodation, psychosocial support, legal information, police or protection services where appropriate. Explain that accepting one service does not require accepting all others.
Make a warm referral when consent is given: confirm the service is open, accessible and safe; explain what to expect; and avoid sending the survivor repeatedly between agencies.
Agree on follow-up and a safe way to communicate. Do not leave identifying messages, send revealing notifications or store files under obvious names if devices may be monitored.
Safety and quality checks
Do not confront the suspected perpetrator, mediate a violent relationship, promise an outcome you cannot control, or pressure a survivor to leave immediately.
Do not use unverified phone numbers or referrals. Services may close, change eligibility rules or share information in unsafe ways; confirm details before publication or referral.
Organisations should train staff, supervise difficult cases, create confidential documentation rules, maintain updated referral maps and offer staff support to reduce burnout and harmful practice.
Action checklist

Have urgent injuries, pregnancy concerns, sexual-violence care and suicide risk been considered?
Has the survivor chosen what information may be recorded or shared?
Are interpretation, disability access, childcare, transport and cost barriers addressed?
Are referrals verified and is there a safe follow-up plan?
Has the person been told that the violence is not her fault and that she can decline any option?

items.title: Caring for women subjected to violence: a WHO curriculum for training health-care providers
items.author: WHO · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A training guide for health-care providers on recognising violence, offering first-line support, providing clinical care and connecting women with safe services.
Key guidance
Create private consultation conditions and never ask about violence when a partner, relative or interpreter chosen by the partner is present.
Use first-line support: listen closely, inquire about needs, validate, enhance safety and connect to support.
Ask only when clinically relevant and when a safe response pathway exists; routine questioning without capacity to respond can cause harm.
Assess immediate danger, threats, weapons, stalking, strangulation, escalating violence and threats involving children.
Treat injuries and health consequences without making police reporting a condition of care.
Document objectively, securely and with consent; distinguish observations from allegations and avoid judgmental language.
Explain confidentiality and mandatory-reporting limits before disclosure, including special rules affecting children or people lacking capacity.
Practise through supervised role-play, reflection and referral exercises; provider attitudes and bias directly affect quality of care.

items.title: Clinical management of rape and intimate partner violence survivors
items.author: WHO, UNFPA and UNHCR · English
sections: Purpose and scope
Clinical guidance for compassionate, evidence-based care after rape and intimate-partner violence, including urgent treatment, documentation and follow-up.
Key guidance
Address life-threatening conditions first while preserving dignity, privacy and the survivor’s control over each examination step.
Obtain informed consent separately for examination, evidence collection, treatment, photographs and information sharing; consent may be withdrawn.
Offer time-sensitive pregnancy prevention, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and sexually transmitted infection care according to current national protocols.
Do not perform virginity testing; it has no scientific validity and can cause physical and psychological harm.
Use trauma-informed examination: explain each step, minimise repetition, allow a support person if desired and stop when asked.
Forensic evidence collection must follow local law, chain-of-custody rules and available laboratory capacity; medical care must never depend on evidence collection.
Assess mental health, acute stress, self-harm risk and social needs without pathologising expected trauma responses.
Plan follow-up for test results, vaccinations, medication adherence, pregnancy, healing, mental health and safe referral.

items.title: Strengthening Health System Responses to Gender-based Violence in Eastern Europe and Central Asia
items.author: UNFPA and WAVE · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A systems guide for strengthening health-sector responses to gender-based violence across policy, facilities, workforce, financing, data and referral networks.
Key guidance
Adopt national clinical protocols, ethical standards and clear roles across primary care, hospitals, emergency care and specialised services.
Budget for private rooms, trained staff, interpretation, essential medicines, forensic supplies where appropriate and referral coordination.
Integrate response into routine health services without labelling records or appointments in ways that expose survivors.
Train whole teams, including reception, security, clinicians, managers and interpreters; a single trained provider cannot fix an unsafe facility.
Build formal referral pathways with shelters, psychosocial services, legal aid and child protection, while verifying quality and confidentiality.
Collect only data needed for care and service improvement; aggregated statistics must not make small communities or individual survivors identifiable.
Monitor access, safety, respectful treatment, waiting time, referral completion and survivor feedback, not only the number of disclosures.
Support providers through supervision, manageable workloads and protocols for staff who experience violence themselves.

items.title: Gender-Based Violence in Emergencies: Operational Guide
items.author: UNICEF · English
sections: Purpose and scope
Operational guidance for preventing and responding to gender-based violence in humanitarian emergencies from preparedness through acute response and recovery.
Key guidance
Assume gender-based violence is occurring even when incident data are incomplete; lack of reports often reflects danger and weak services.
Include women and girls in assessment and programme design using safe, accessible methods that do not demand disclosure of personal violence.
Reduce risks in water, sanitation, shelter, food distribution, cash programmes, transport and camp layout.
Establish confidential case management, health care, psychosocial support and safe referral routes early in the response.
Never make assistance conditional on reporting violence, producing documents, meeting alone with staff or accepting a referral.
Use safe feedback and complaints channels and enforce protection from sexual exploitation and abuse by personnel and partners.
Plan for adolescents, older women, women with disabilities, displaced people, minorities and LGBTQI persons whose access and risks differ.
Coordinate across sectors while sharing the minimum identifiable information and avoiding public lists of survivors.

items.title: Essential Services Package for Women and Girls Subject to Violence
items.author: UN Women, UNFPA, WHO, UNDP and UNODC · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A coordinated package defining the essential health, police, justice and social services women and girls should be able to access after violence.
Key guidance
Core health services include first-line support, injury care, sexual and reproductive health care, mental-health support, documentation and referral.
Social services should provide crisis information, safe accommodation, counselling, material help, child support and longer-term recovery options.
Police response should prioritise safety, respectful communication, risk assessment, evidence preservation and enforcement of protection measures.
Justice services should provide accessible information, legal assistance, timely procedures, privacy and remedies without blaming survivors.
Coordination requires agreed protocols, named contacts, secure referral methods and accountability when a service fails.
Services should be available regardless of income, disability, nationality, marital status, sexual orientation or willingness to pursue a criminal case.
Quality depends on informed consent, confidentiality, cultural safety, competent staff and regular survivor-informed evaluation.
A case should not be closed merely because a survivor declines one option or returns to a partner; continued respectful access matters.

items.title: Intensifying efforts to eliminate violence against women and girls
items.author: UN Secretary-General · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A global policy review identifying progress, persistent gaps and priority actions needed to eliminate violence against women and girls.
Key guidance
Strong laws require implementation plans, budgets, trained institutions and remedies; legislation alone does not guarantee safety.
Prevention should address unequal power, discriminatory norms, economic insecurity, conflict, online abuse and institutional impunity.
States need accessible multisectoral services in urban, rural and remote areas, including long-term housing and economic recovery.
Reliable prevalence and administrative data should be collected ethically, disaggregated carefully and protected from misuse.
Women’s rights organisations need predictable, flexible funding and meaningful participation in policy decisions.
Technology companies and governments should address online threats, image-based abuse, stalking and platform-enabled harassment while protecting expression and privacy.
Conflict, displacement, climate shocks and political repression increase risks and require tailored prevention and services.
Accountability mechanisms should measure real access, survivor safety and reductions in violence, not only policies adopted or people trained.

items.title: General recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women
items.author: UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A human-rights explanation of state obligations under CEDAW regarding gender-based violence against women in public, private, physical and digital settings.
Key guidance
Gender-based violence is a form of discrimination that can violate rights to life, health, liberty, equality, privacy and freedom from torture.
State responsibility includes acts by public authorities and failures to exercise due diligence regarding violence by private persons or organisations.
Obligations cover prevention, protection, investigation, punishment, reparation and measures addressing structural inequality.
Laws and procedures should not rely on stereotypes about how a “real victim” behaves, delay in reporting, sexual history or family roles.
Intersectional discrimination can intensify risk and barriers for disabled, migrant, Indigenous, minority, lesbian, bisexual and transgender women.
Reparations may include compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction, guarantees of non-repetition and structural reform.
Data collection, courts, policing, health care and education must comply with confidentiality, equality and non-discrimination.
Restrictions justified by culture, religion, tradition or “family honour” cannot excuse violence or unequal protection.

items.title: How to support survivors when a specialist is unavailable
items.author: UNICEF and IASC partners · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A pocket guide for any humanitarian worker or community member who receives a disclosure when no specialised gender-based-violence service is available.
Key guidance
Prepare before a disclosure: know available health, safety, child-protection and emergency services and understand which referrals may be unsafe.
Introduce your role and limits, find a private setting, and check whether continuing the conversation is safe.
Listen calmly, believe the person, acknowledge her courage and ask what she needs now; avoid “why” questions and detailed fact-finding.
Do not search for survivors, investigate, mediate, contact the alleged perpetrator or publicly identify someone as a survivor.
Share accurate information in a language and format the person can understand, including the right to decline services.
For children, follow child-safeguarding procedures and involve trained actors; do not make promises of secrecy that conflict with clear protection duties.
If no specialist exists, identify safe general services and community supports without disclosing the reason for referral unnecessarily.
After the conversation, store no unnecessary notes, consult supervision without identifying details and care for your own wellbeing.

items.title: Innovative approaches to GBV service provision in emergencies
items.author: UNICEF · English
sections: Purpose and scope
Examples and safeguards for adapting gender-based-violence services during emergencies, lockdowns and movement restrictions.
Key guidance
Remote case management should be offered only after checking device access, surveillance risks, privacy, connectivity and the survivor’s preferred contact method.
Use neutral appointment names, agreed code words, safe times and rapid-exit plans; never assume a personal phone is private.
Maintain in-person options for people without safe technology, literacy, disability access, money, identification or stable connectivity.
Pharmacies, health facilities, cash programmes and community networks may support discreet referrals only with training and strict confidentiality.
Digital tools should collect the minimum data, use role-based access, avoid unsafe cloud backups and have a breach-response plan.
Staff need protocols for interrupted calls, imminent danger, child safeguarding, cross-border referrals and technology failure.
Monitor whether adaptations exclude groups or increase control by perpetrators; convenience for providers is not evidence of safety.
Document innovations, survivor feedback and adverse effects so temporary measures improve rather than weaken service quality.

items.title: Virtual safe spaces for women and girls
items.author: UNICEF · English
sections: Purpose and scope
Design principles for virtual safe spaces that connect women and girls with information, peer support and services when physical spaces are limited.
Key guidance
Co-design the space with diverse women and girls and test assumptions about devices, data costs, literacy, disability and privacy.
Choose platforms based on threat assessment, not popularity; consider account discovery, metadata, screenshots, impersonation and group-member visibility.
Minimise registration data, explain moderation and reporting, and give users control over notifications and account deletion.
Provide a prominent safe-exit function and neutral screen content, while explaining that browser history and device monitoring may still reveal use.
Moderators need safeguarding training, escalation protocols, boundaries and supervision; a virtual group is not automatically a confidential space.
Separate general information from individual case management and never invite public disclosure of identifying experiences.
Offer low-tech and offline alternatives and avoid excluding women who share devices or cannot read.
Evaluate safety incidents, accessibility, trust, useful referrals and user control rather than counting logins alone.

items.title: Istanbul Convention: Questions and Answers
items.author: Council of Europe · English
sections: Purpose and scope
A question-and-answer guide to the Istanbul Convention and its framework for prevention, protection, prosecution and coordinated policy.
Key guidance
The Convention treats violence against women as a human-rights violation and a manifestation of historically unequal power.
It covers prevention, survivor protection and support, substantive law, investigation, prosecution and integrated policy.
States should provide information, shelters, helplines, health care, specialist support, rape crisis services and protection for child witnesses.
Support should not depend on a survivor pressing charges or testifying, and services should avoid discrimination.
The Convention does not prescribe family structures or require teaching a particular lifestyle; it addresses harmful stereotypes that normalise violence.
Monitoring by GREVIO examines laws, implementation and practice and includes evidence from civil society.
Risk assessment, emergency barring orders and protection orders should respond quickly while respecting survivor safety and procedural rights.
Migration and asylum procedures should recognise gender-based persecution and avoid exposing applicants to further harm.
